column1: What is the eBPF register architecture (count and bit-width)?
column2: A 64-bit RISC virtual machine with 11 general-purpose registers, R0 through R10 (R0 is the return value register, R10 is the read-only frame pointer).

column1: What three properties must an eBPF program prove to pass the kernel verifier?
column2: Termination (no unbounded loops), memory safety (no out-of-bounds accesses), and type safety (no arbitrary pointer arithmetic).

column1: Why does the eBPF verifier frequently reject loops, and what is the common error message?
column2: The verifier must prove bounded execution time via DAG analysis of all paths; unbounded loops violate this, producing the error 'back-edge from insn X to insn Y'.

column1: What is the founding invariant of Cilium's security model compared to traditional firewalls?
column2: Authorization is based on workload identity (derived from labels), not network location (IP address) — 'what a workload is' rather than 'where it is running'.

column1: How does Cilium derive a security identity for a pod?
column2: It captures the pod's Kubernetes labels at endpoint creation and distills them into a numeric security identity, consistent cluster-wide and persistent for the lifetime of that labeled pod set.

column1: Why does a pod rescheduling event not require any firewall rule updates in Cilium?
column2: Because security identity is derived from immutable labels, not the ephemeral IP address; when the pod moves and gets a new IP, its identity (and thus policy treatment) remains unchanged.

column1: What is the bit-width of Cilium security identities, and what backs their cluster-wide consistency?
column2: 24-bit unsigned integers, managed by the Cilium operator through etcd-backed consensus to guarantee cluster-wide uniqueness.

column1: Contrast the lookup complexity of traditional iptables policy evaluation vs. Cilium's identity-based eBPF policy evaluation.
column2: Iptables: O(n) sequential rule-chain traversal over five-tuple matches. Cilium: O(1) constant-time hash table lookup keyed on resolved security identity pairs.

column1: What three distinct problems must be solved when a pod sends traffic to a ClusterIP service?
column2: 1) Destination NAT (translating ClusterIP to real endpoint IP), 2) Load balancing (selecting a backend), 3) Session affinity/connection tracking (keeping subsequent packets on the same backend).

column1: In the iptables kube-proxy model, how are DNAT state, backend selection, and stickiness implemented?
column2: DNAT state is held in the conntrack table, backend selection uses probability-match rules for randomized selection, and their interaction produces per-connection stickiness.

column1: What architectural shift does Cilium's kube-proxy replacement make regarding the service forwarding plane?
column2: It replaces linear iptables chains with eBPF programs at well-defined hook points backed by BPF maps offering O(1) lookup, with observability built directly into the same forwarding code paths.

column1: What four kernel config options must be enabled for Cilium's eBPF subsystem to function, and what CLI command reports agent health?
column2: CONFIG_BPF_SYSCALL, CONFIG_BPF_JIT, CONFIG_CGROUP_BPF (plus related BPF support); health is checked via `cilium status`, which should report KVStore: Ok, Kubernetes: Ok, Cilium: Ok, and IPAM status.
